guide.title: Ludovisi, Rome: Via Veneto, the Capuchin Crypt and the Villa That Was Sold Off
guide.intro: Ludovisi is one of Rome's rioni. Roma Capitale's Annuario statistico 2022 gives it the toponymic code 116, and Roma Capitale's roster of rioni places it in Municipio I. Almost all of it was built after 1886, when the Boncompagni Ludovisi heirs, the Comune and the Società Generale Immobiliare signed the convention that put the park of Villa Ludovisi to subdivision; Italian Wikipedia's article on Palazzo Margherita says the quarter that replaced the park was constituted as a rione in 1921. What stands there now is a grid of wide streets around via Vittorio Veneto, built up with hotels, ministries, embassies and villini, and a great deal of it cannot be entered: the United States Embassy occupies Palazzo Margherita, and Roma Capitale says plainly that it is closed to the public. What you can go into here is mostly churches, one ossuary crypt and one Swiss cultural institute.

sections.heading: Villa Ludovisi, and what happened to it
sections.body:
Everything in this rione begins with a garden that no longer exists. Italian Wikipedia records that Cardinal Ludovico Ludovisi, nephew of Gregory XV, bought the Villa Orsini in 1622 and enlarged it with adjoining properties, over the ground of the Horti Sallustiani; Roma Capitale's via Veneto page instead dates his purchase of the Horti land to 1621. The buildings were designed by Domenichino, who is credited with at least part of the gardens too on the strength of Bellori (1672), Malvasia (1678), Sebastiani (1683) and Milizia (1768); later writers attribute the gardens instead to André Le Nôtre, on the strength of Milizia's own Memorie of 1781. Italian Wikipedia presents that as an unsettled scholarly dispute, and so does this guide.

The villa's extent is reported variously: Italian Wikipedia's article on the villa gives 30 hectares, its article on the rione says the 1886 convention put about 25 hectares of park to subdivision, and the Boncompagni Ludovisi family's own archive at villaludovisi.org gives 89.6 acres. Subdivision was decided in 1883, and Italian Wikipedia's articles on the villa and on the rione both date the convention with the Comune and the Società Generale Immobiliare to 1886, signed sotto gli auspici del sindaco di Roma, duca Leopoldo Torlonia. Its article on Palazzo Margherita dates that convention to 1883 instead; the two dates come from two articles and this guide does not pick between them.

The gardens, the casini and the palazzo were mostly not spared. Italian Wikipedia says the cardinal's collection ran to more than 450 antique sculptures, that a hundred or so were bought by the Italian state in 1910 and first placed in the Piccolo Chiostro at Santa Maria degli Angeli, and that the collection is not in Ludovisi. The Trono Ludovisi was not part of that collection: Italian Wikipedia records that it was found in 1887, during the destruction of the villa. What survives on the ground is the Casino dell'Aurora, and the trees of two gardens.

sections.heading: Via Veneto
sections.body:
Via Vittorio Veneto, universally called via Veneto, climbs from Piazza Barberini to Porta Pinciana. Italian Wikipedia files the street under two rioni, Colonna and Ludovisi, and states that along its opening stretch the street separates the one from the other; its upper length runs through Ludovisi. Roma Capitale dates the street's creation to 1894, when it was laid out as a broad passeggiata Umbertina during the building-over of Villa Ludovisi; Italian Wikipedia's rione article instead says the street was completed in 1906. It was renamed for the battle of Vittorio Veneto by resolution of the Giunta Municipale, no. 37 of 25 October 1919. Roma Capitale records that the street's international fame rests on the Dolce Vita, and states that Fellini rebuilt via Veneto in the studios at Cinecittà rather than filming on it.

Roma Capitale records that the Hotel Excelsior on via Veneto was inaugurated in 1906 by Baron von Pfyffer, the owner of the Grand Hotel, among the first-class hotels built along the new street. Via Veneto ends at the Aurelian Walls, at the largo named for Federico Fellini. This guide publishes no length for the street, because the figure that circulates is an unreferenced Wikipedia infobox value, and it claims neither the street nor the gate at the top of it as a place: Roma Capitale publishes a via Veneto address for Porta Pinciana together with a coordinate that falls in the quartiere Pinciano, and Italian Wikipedia's boundary description makes the walls up to that gate the rione's edge rather than something inside it.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Via Veneto climbs from Piazza Barberini to Porta Pinciana, so arriving at the bottom means walking up and leaving from the top means walking down.

Four of the five borders run down the middle of a street, which is worth knowing before you trust a map pin. Italian Wikipedia describes the perimeter as the Aurelian Walls up to Porta Pinciana with the quartiere Pinciano; via di Porta Pinciana and via Francesco Crispi with Campo Marzio; via degli Artisti, via di Sant'Isidoro and via Veneto with Colonna; via di San Basilio with Trevi; and via Friuli, via Lucullo, via Boncompagni and via Calabria as far as piazza Fiume, excluded, with Sallustiano. The Sallustiano article gives the same line from the other side. On via Boncompagni the odd numbers are Ludovisi and the even numbers Sallustiano: St Patrick's, at no. 31, is in this rione, and the Museo Boncompagni Ludovisi, at no. 18, is not.

faq.question: Can you go inside Palazzo Margherita?
faq.answer: No. Roma Capitale states that the palace is closed to the public and can be seen only from outside. It is the diplomatic mission of the United States in Italy: it stands on Italian soil and is subject to Italian law, and its premises are inviolable under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, which is an obligation on Italy rather than a transfer of sovereignty. The palace is not United States territory.

faq.question: What are the opening hours of the Capuchin crypt?
faq.answer: The museum's own site gives the hours as every day 09:30-13:30 and 14:30-18:30, with last admissions at 12:30 and 17:30, and the telephone as 06 88803695. The same page says the museum closes at 13:30 on Holy Saturday, 2 November, 24 December and 31 December, and does not open on Easter Sunday, 25 December or 1 January. Hours change; check the museum's site before going.

faq.question: Can you visit the Casino dell'Aurora?
faq.answer: This guide cannot tell you. The building is private. Italian Wikipedia records that it was put up for auction after an inheritance dispute, that every auction held between January 2022 and January 2023 drew no bidder, that Princess Rita Boncompagni Ludovisi was evicted by court order on 20 April 2023, and that in July 2023 the heirs agreed to sell it privately instead. Whether and on what terms it can be visited is not established by any source, and this guide states no opening arrangements for it. The family archive at villaludovisi.org still describes the Princess as living there and is out of date on that point.

faq.question: Is the Museo Boncompagni Ludovisi in Ludovisi?
faq.answer: No, despite the name. It is at Via Boncompagni 18, in the Villino Boncompagni Ludovisi, and via Boncompagni is the boundary street: the even numbers are in Sallustiano. Italian Wikipedia files the museum under its Sallustiano category.

faq.question: Why does one small rione have so many foreign churches?
faq.answer: Two of them are national churches, one is owned by an Irish order, and one is a foreign-language congregation. Italian Wikipedia records that Sant'Isidoro a Capo le Case passed to the Irish Franciscans two years after its foundation and that they own it still; that San Patrizio became the national parish of Americans resident in Rome on 1 August 2017, when the Paulist Fathers moved into it; and that San Marone is the national church of Lebanon, served by Maronites of Lebanon in the Antiochene rite in Arabic. The Lutheran Christuskirche on via Sicilia is the fourth, built to the design of Wilhelm II's court architect and run by a congregation whose own site is in German and Italian.

faq.question: Was La Dolce Vita filmed on via Veneto?
faq.answer: Roma Capitale ties the street's international fame to the Dolce Vita, and states that Fellini rebuilt via Veneto in the studios at Cinecittà rather than filming on the street itself. Italian Wikipedia records the Cafe de Paris, one of the cafes the film made famous, as closed in 2008.

photos.title: Santa Maria della Concezione dei Cappuccini
photos.description: The brick facade of the Capuchin church at Via Vittorio Veneto 27, reached by the double scissor stair that carries visitors up from the street to the church and the ossuary crypt beneath it.
photos.author: José Luiz

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria della Concezione dei Cappuccini
places.summary: The Capuchin church on the lower part of via Veneto, and the reason the ossuary crypt beneath it is here. Roma Capitale records that it was built at the instance of the Capuchin cardinal Antonio Barberini, brother of Urban VIII, who blessed the first stone on 4 October 1626, to a design by the pontifical architect Michele da Bergamo with Antonio Casoni; Italian Wikipedia dates the construction 1626-1631. One nave, five chapels to a side, reached by a scissor stair, behind a brick façade with white stone pilasters. Roma Capitale records its dedication to the Immaculate Conception.
places.history: Cardinal Barberini's tomb is in front of the high altar, inscribed Hic jacet pulvis et cinis et nihil. Roma Capitale names the paintings: Guido Reni's San Michele Arcangelo, Pietro da Cortona's Anania che ridà la vista a San Paolo, Andrea Sacchi's Sant'Antonio da Padova resuscita un morto, Gherardo delle Notti's Cristo deriso, Lanfranco's Adorazione dei Pastori and Domenichino's San Francesco d'Assisi sorretto dall'Angelo; Italian Wikipedia dates Liborio Coccetti's Assunzione on the barrel vault to 1796. Italian Wikipedia records that the sacristy, now a museum, holds a San Francesco in meditazione recently attributed to Caravaggio. The attribution is recent and is not settled. The same article records that the friars' old convent was demolished in the 1920s to make room for the Ministry of Corporations, which is the Palazzo Piacentini also described in this guide, and that the convent was promptly rebuilt beside the church in 1925. Italian Wikipedia gives the church complex's official site as cappucciniviaveneto.it, a different domain from the museum's.

places.name: Museo e Cripta dei Cappuccini
places.summary: The Capuchins' museum and ossuary crypt, in the same complex as the church above and sold on its own ticket. The museum's own site gives the address as Via Vittorio Veneto 27, 00187 Roma, the telephone as 06 88803695, and the hours as every day 09:30-13:30 and 14:30-18:30, with last admissions at 12:30 and 17:30. It also states that the museum closes at 13:30 on Holy Saturday, 2 November, 24 December and 31 December, and does not open on Easter Sunday, 25 December or 1 January, and it describes itself as a museum associated with AMEI. Tickets are sold online, and the site advertises evening visits. Hours change; check the site before going.
places.history: Roma Capitale describes the crypt as the Capuchins' former cemetery, realizzata verso la prima metà del XVIII secolo, five chapels decorated with the skulls and bones of about 4,000 friars, each chapel named for the bones used to decorate it, and each said by tradition to hold holy earth brought from Palestine or Jerusalem. Italian Wikipedia adds a separate fact that is easy to confuse with the first: the bones themselves were gathered between 1528 and 1870, from the order's old cemetery at Santa Croce e San Bonaventura dei Lucchesi. The making of the crypt and the gathering of the bones are two different dates and this guide keeps them apart. Italian Wikipedia quotes the plaque at the entrance: Quello che voi siete noi eravamo; quello che noi siamo voi sarete.

places.name: Palazzo Margherita
places.summary: The palace on via Veneto that is now the Embassy of the United States of America. Roma Capitale places it inside Rione XVI - Ludovisi and states that it is closed to the public and can be seen only from outside. Roma Capitale names one work inside it, a Venus by Giambologna carved in 1583 and known as the Venere Cesarini.
places.history:
Palazzo Margherita was built to Gaetano Koch's design for Rodolfo Boncompagni Ludovisi, Prince of Piombino, on the ground of the Villa Ludovisi his family was subdividing; Roma Capitale gives the date as 1890 and Italian Wikipedia as 1886-1890. Italian Wikipedia records that the prince built it to replace Palazzo Piombino on via del Corso, from which he had been expropriated, and that the building incorporates at its rear the Palazzo Grande of 1622, the original nucleus of the villa, which Italian Wikipedia says is neither visitable nor visible from the street. The palace passed to the House of Savoy in 1900 and was the residence of the Queen Mother Margherita, from whom it takes its name, until her death in 1926. Accounts of the American tenancy differ: Roma Capitale says the Embassy of the United States has been here since the end of the Second World War, while Italian Wikipedia says the palace became the Embassy in 1931 and was bought by the United States Government in 1946. Italian Wikipedia records that the trees of this garden and those of the Casino dell'Aurora are the last remnant of the villa's park.

The building is the diplomatic mission of the United States in Italy. It stands on Italian soil and is subject to Italian law. Its premises are inviolable under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, which binds Italy to protect them; that is an obligation on Italy, not a transfer of sovereignty, and the palace is not United States territory.

Roma Capitale states that the palace is closed to the public and can be seen only from outside.

places.name: Casino dell'Aurora
places.summary: The Casino dell'Aurora, also called Casino Ludovisi or Villa Aurora, on via Aurora, is a building of Villa Ludovisi that survives intact. Italian Wikipedia records that it was built for Cardinal Francesco Maria Del Monte in the sixteenth century and remodelled for Ludovico Ludovisi between 1621 and 1632, and that it takes its name from Guercino's Aurora on the vault of the ground-floor salone. Italian Wikipedia also records that the building holds a wall painting by Caravaggio, Giove, Nettuno e Plutone, painted for Del Monte between 1597 and 1600, and a triptych by Guercino and Tassi on the piano nobile.
places.history:
The building is private. Italian Wikipedia records that it was put up for auction after an inheritance dispute, that every auction held between January 2022 and January 2023 drew no bidder, that Princess Rita Boncompagni Ludovisi was evicted by court order on 20 April 2023, and that in July 2023 the heirs agreed to sell it privately instead. Whether and on what terms it can be visited is not established by any source, and this guide does not state opening arrangements for it. The Boncompagni Ludovisi family archive at villaludovisi.org, which is excellent on the family's documents, still describes the Princess as living in the building and is out of date on occupancy.

One warning about the name. Rome has two buildings called Casino dell'Aurora, in two different rioni, and Italian Wikipedia carries a disambiguation page rather than an article at that title; the Ludovisi one is covered inside its Villa Ludovisi article. Italian Wikipedia dates Guercino's Aurora here to 1621, and Guido Reni's Aurora, in the other building at Palazzo Pallavicini Rospigliosi, to 1614.

places.name: Villa Maraini (Istituto Svizzero)
places.summary: An eclectic villa with neo-Baroque elements, standing on an artificial hill made from the spoil of the excavation of via Ludovisi, with a garden and a grotto nymphaeum and a Torre Belvedere 26 metres high. Roma Capitale says the villa sorge nel Rione Ludovisi, and records that it was built between 1903 and 1905 by the Ticinese architect Otto Maraini for his brother Emilio, the industrialist who introduced beet-sugar production to Italy. Roma Capitale calls the building Villa Maraini; Italian Wikipedia's text and infobox, and the rione's own article, call it Villino Maraini.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that Emilio Maraini's widow, Countess Carolina Maraini-Sommaruga, gave the villa to the Swiss Confederation in 1946 on the condition that it be perpetuamente al servizio della cultura, nel segno della collaborazione tra la Svizzera e l'Italia. Roma Capitale's page on the Istituto Svizzero says the institute has been active since 1947; Italian Wikipedia says the villa was entrusted to it in 1948, when it established its seat here. Roma Capitale states that the institute organises guided visits inside the villa. The institute's own site gives the address as Via Ludovisi 48, the telephone as +39 06 420 421, and says guided visits are by booking only, through visite@istitutosvizzero.it. Check the institute's site before going, which is what Roma Capitale itself advises.

places.name: Palazzo Piacentini
places.summary: The ministry building on the corner of via Molise and via Veneto, by Marcello Piacentini and Giuseppe Vaccaro, inaugurated in 1932 as the Palazzo delle Corporazioni and now the seat of the Ministero delle Imprese e del Made in Italy. Roma Capitale publishes the address as Via Molise 2; Italian Wikipedia's infobox gives via Veneto 33, which is the same corner building. Italian Wikipedia dates the construction 1928-1932 and says it was raised on the ground formerly occupied by the convent and vegetable garden of the Capuchins of Santa Maria della Concezione. It is not the Palazzo Piacentini in via Arenula, which is by Pio Piacentini; Italian Wikipedia warns about the confusion in terms.
places.history:
Roma Capitale lists what is inside: Mario Sironi's polychrome window Carta del Lavoro, Ferruccio Ferrazzi's tapestries in the salone d'onore, Enrico Prampolini's Madonna dell'Aria, Fortunato Depero's Sintesi Veneziana, Giovanni Prini's bronze doors on via Veneto, Carlo Pini's sculptures in the atrium, and the Parlamentino, a hemicycle room ancora utilizzato per le riunioni del Dicastero. Italian Wikipedia adds Antonio Maraini and Ercole Drei to the list of artists.

The ministry states that the palace can be visited only by appointment, on a free guided tour arranged through its Polo culturale at Via Molise 2, with the full list of the group, no more than 25 to 30 people, sent at least fifteen days in advance. Check the ministry's current site for the booking address before going: the URL Roma Capitale prints, and the email address it gives, are both on the ministry's superseded domain.

places.name: Chiesa di Sant'Isidoro a Capo le Case
places.summary: A church and convent above a double flight of steps, owned by Irish Franciscans. Italian Wikipedia records that it was founded on the munificence of Ottaviano Vestri di Barbiano, per a bull of Urban VIII of 1625, and built for Gregory XV's canonisation in 1622 of five saints including the Spaniard Isidore the Farmer; Spanish Discalced Franciscans came to Rome that year to found a house and raised the church. After two years the church and convent passed to the Irish Franciscans, who had fled persecution and who, Italian Wikipedia says, are the owners still. Its infobox gives 1622-1672 for the building.
places.history:
Italian Wikipedia credits the fabric to Antonio Felice Casoni and then Domenico Castelli, with the façade, its portico and its double flight of steps by Carlo Francesco Bizzaccheri in 1704-1705. Inside are works by Carlo Maratta, including an Immacolata Concezione in the De Sylva chapel whose picture frame was designed by Bernini; the chapel itself was remodelled to Bernini's design, and the funerary monuments in it are by his son Paolo Valentino Bernini. Andrea Sacchi painted the high altarpiece. There are two cloisters: the small one is by Casoni, in 1626, and the second is named for Luke Wadding. Italian Wikipedia records that the convent housed the Nazarenes, the proto-Romantic and mostly German painters, some of them resident between 1810 and Pius VII's return in 1814, and that via degli Artisti takes its name from them.

One honest note on where this church is. Italian Wikipedia files it under its Ludovisi churches category, which is why this guide carries it. But the streets it stands on are the boundary with Colonna, and Armellini's Le chiese di Roma dal secolo IV al XIX of 1891, which Italian Wikipedia links in its own bibliography for the church, filed it under rione Colonna. The modern evidence decides it here; the older evidence is recorded rather than hidden. No source gives an official website for this church, and santisidoro.org belongs to a different organisation, a cultural association in Marano di Napoli.

places.name: Chiesa di San Patrizio a Villa Ludovisi
places.summary: The national parish of Americans resident in Rome, and the church in this rione where everything happens in English. Italian Wikipedia records that it was built in 1908 to the design of Aristide Leonori, neo-Renaissance with Romanesque-Byzantine motifs on the façade, with three naves and a coffered ceiling. The parish's own site gives the address as Via Boncompagni 31. Check the parish site for opening times before going.
places.history:
Italian Wikipedia records the apse mosaic San Patrizio che predica alle folle by Rodolfo Villani, 1929, the apse inscription Ut cristiani ita et romani sitis, and a sixteenth-century Madonna delle grazie over the high altar which came from the now-vanished church of Santa Maria in Posterula.

The church changed hands within living memory, and Italian Wikipedia, citing the National Catholic Reporter, dates it exactly. It belonged to the Irish Augustinians until 2017. From 1 August 2017 it passed to the Paulist Fathers, who moved here from Santa Susanna, their seat since 1922, and from that date it became the national parish of Americans resident in Rome in place of Santa Susanna. All Masses are in English. One source trap worth naming: stpatricksrome.com is a parked domain offered for sale and is not the parish; the parish's site is stpatricksamericanrome.org.

places.name: Chiesa evangelica luterana (Christuskirche)
places.summary: The Lutheran church of Rome, built between 1910 and 1922 and opened in 1922, to the design of Franz Heinrich Schwechten, court architect to Wilhelm II and architect of Berlin's Kaiser-Wilhelm-Gedächtniskirche. Roma Capitale describes a gabled façade of squared stone on via Sicilia between two square bell towers, with three marble statues over the portico: Christ in the centre, St Peter to the left, St Paul to the right. Roma Capitale publishes the address as Via Sicilia 70 and says the façade gives onto via Sicilia; the building is on a corner and geocoders resolve it to via Toscana.
places.history:
Roma Capitale records that during construction, at a depth of 2.40 metres, the paving of a Roman road four metres wide was found. It also records that a thirteen-metre Roman obelisk from the Villa of Sallust, the Horti Sallustiani, was found in this part of the city in the nineteenth century, and that it now stands in front of Trinità dei Monti.

Inside, per Roma Capitale: three naves with matronei, an apse mosaic of the Tree of Life with Christ Pantocrator in a mandorla, a font modelled on that of the Dómkirkjan in Reykjavík, and a Steinmeyer organ, opus 1515, built in 1930, with 35 stops, two 61-note manuals and a 30-note pedalboard. Roma Capitale records three papal visits, all dated: John Paul II on 11 December 1983, Benedict XVI on 14 March 2010 and Francis on 15 November 2015. The congregation's own site, ev-luth-gemeinde-rom.org, is live and bilingual in German and Italian.

places.name: Chiesa di San Marone
places.summary: The Maronite national church of Lebanon. Italian Wikipedia records that it was built in 1890 to the design of Andrea Busiri Vici, and that it is dedicated to the fifth-century Syrian hermit who founded the Maronite Church. It is served by Maronites of Lebanon, in the Antiochene rite, in Arabic.
places.history: Italian Wikipedia records that the Maronite monastery attached to the church was converted into a hotel in 1936. This is a short entry because the sources are short: the church has a five-line article on Italian Wikipedia, and no source names an official site for it. What it is and where it is are established; nothing else about it is.

entries.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria della Concezione dei Cappuccini
entries.note: Cardinal Antonio Barberini blessed the first stone on 4 October 1626; one nave and five chapels a side, with paintings by Guido Reni, Pietro da Cortona and Domenichino.

entries.name: Museo e Cripta dei Cappuccini
entries.note: Five chapels decorated with the skulls and bones of about 4,000 friars, gathered between 1528 and 1870, on a ticket of their own; hours change, so check the museum's site.

entries.name: Palazzo Margherita
entries.note: Gaetano Koch built it on the ground of the villa the Boncompagni Ludovisi were subdividing; it housed the Queen Mother Margherita until 1926 and is now the United States Embassy, closed to the public and seen only from outside.

entries.name: Casino dell'Aurora
entries.note: The building of Villa Ludovisi that survives intact, with Guercino's Aurora on the salone vault; it is private, and no source establishes whether it can be entered.

entries.name: Villa Maraini (Istituto Svizzero)
entries.note: Raised 1903-1905 on an artificial hill of spoil from the digging of via Ludovisi, with a 26-metre Torre Belvedere; the Swiss Institute runs guided visits inside, by booking only.

entries.name: Palazzo Piacentini
entries.note: Inaugurated 1932 as the Palazzo delle Corporazioni, with Sironi's Carta del Lavoro window and Prini's bronze doors on via Veneto; visits are by appointment, arranged at least fifteen days ahead.

entries.name: Chiesa di Sant'Isidoro a Capo le Case
entries.note: Irish Franciscans took it two years after the 1622 foundation and own it still; Bizzaccheri built the façade, portico and double stair in 1704-1705, and the De Sylva chapel was remodelled to Bernini's design.

entries.name: Chiesa di San Patrizio a Villa Ludovisi
entries.note: Aristide Leonori's church of 1908, with Villani's 1929 apse mosaic; the Paulist Fathers arrived on 1 August 2017 and all Masses are in English.

entries.name: Chiesa evangelica luterana (Christuskirche)
entries.note: Opened in 1922 to a design by Wilhelm II's court architect, with an apse mosaic of the Tree of Life, a font modelled on Reykjavík's and a Steinmeyer organ of 1930.

links.note: Via Boncompagni is the line between the two rioni, and the Museo Boncompagni Ludovisi, at no. 18, is on Sallustiano's side of it.
The Ludovisi antique sculptures were first placed in the Piccolo Chiostro at Santa Maria degli Angeli, which stands in Castro Pretorio.
